title.analysis: Authentic title "Are You On Track to Becoming a Multi-Millionaire? (2026 Edition)" promises a benchmarking check. The script delivers percentile tables, age medians, savings-rate math and a reframing ("rate, time and friction"; months of runway) rather than a single verdict; it warns that $2M is a middle-class income. The title matches.

script.stored_text_completeness: All 18840 canonical characters read sequentially in full in 1 bounded ranges; auto-generated untimed text; stored text ends on the closing line ("...and then go make it the other one.") with no sign-off; ASR garbles several figures ("1902,900" for $192,900, "985th" for 95th, "2470" for $2,470, "1.2 2 percentage points"); composites Otis, Wanda and Alton; audio, timed delivery and editing unverified.
script.opening_words: Last year, this country minted about 1,200 new millionaires a day, every day, weekends included. And across roughly that same stretch, the wealth of the median American adult fell by about a fifth. Both of those things are true. Both of them came out of the same report. So, somewhere out there is a scoreboard showing the biggest numbers in recorded history hanging over a stadium that keeps getting emptier. Before you ask whether you're on track, you should probably
script.ending_words: reads, "How many months could you stop right now today before something breaks?" For most people, that number is under one. Getting it to three will change your life more than getting it to two million ever will. And unlike 2 million, you can start on it this month. So don't ask whether you're a millionaire yet. Ask which clock is winning and then go make it the other one.
script.analysis: Full 18840 canonical characters read. A single-narrator, data-dense explainer with composites Otis, Wanda and Alton: two clocks (compounding vs cost), SCF percentiles and mean-vs-median, Fidelity/T. Rowe benchmarks, age medians, Vanguard balances and plan access, Wanda's early-start math, the price of delay, Otis's late start, Alton's lifestyle creep, 3.9% withdrawal and tax haircut, Ramsey/Stanley/Ronald Read, inheritance odds, pensions to 401(k)s, asset vs wage growth, wealth shares, $400 SHED, optimistic and pessimistic cases, behaviour gap, and a close on runway months. Most arithmetic reproduces; Alton's outcome does not, and the plan-access figure is overstated.
